Building on the previous unit, where we weighed self-regulation and internal codes of ethics against their limits, we now turn to the hardest instrument in the toolbox: binding EU law. Voluntary commitments can shape a corporate culture, but they cannot be enforced against a firm that decides to ignore them. The EU AI Act is the European legislator's answer to exactly that gap. It regulates a foundational technology of the digital society and its applications, and it does so with an eye on safety, health and fundamental rights.

## Background and legislative history

### A legal framework for trustworthy AI

The EU AI Act, formally Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, is part of a larger Commission package intended to support *trustworthy* artificial intelligence. Alongside the Regulation itself, that package includes the AI innovation package for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and start-ups and the Coordinated Plan on AI. The Commission markets the AI Act confidently as the **first comprehensive legal framework for AI in the world**, even though the Regulation itself leaves several central questions open. This first-mover role is deliberate: the EU wants to set global standards.

One double delimitation matters from the outset. The AI Act contains **no** rules on civil liability for the outcomes of AI, and no substantive intellectual-property provisions either. It is product-safety and fundamental-rights law, not civil liability law. Anyone harmed by an AI system therefore finds their claims not here but in general and specialised liability law, the subject of the next unit.

### From proposal to regulation, and on to its first amendment

The process stretched over more than three years. On **21 April 2021** the Commission tabled its proposal; the project counted as one of the most important regulatory undertakings of the 2019-2024 term. After adoption by Parliament (March 2024) and Council (May 2024), the text was published in the Official Journal on **12 July 2024**. The AI Act **entered into force** on **1 August 2024**.

It has not stayed in that shape. Before the bulk of its obligations had even begun to apply, the AI Act was amended by the **Digital Omnibus on AI**, [Regulation (EU) 2026/1744](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj){target="_blank"} of 8 July 2026, in force since **27 July 2026**. It reaches into roughly seventy places in the AI Act but leaves its architecture, risk tiers and penalty ceilings untouched. This unit states the AI Act **as amended**, flagging where a rule looks the way it does because the Omnibus made it so.

::: {.flip-card}
#### Digital Omnibus on AI
Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026. An amending regulation, not a new act: it simplifies implementation of the AI Act without lowering the substantive protection level, chiefly by postponing the high-risk obligations and centralising enforcement for the largest providers.
:::

## Scope and definitions

### Territorial: a broad marketplace principle

The territorial scope is drawn deliberately wide ([Art. 2 AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}). The Regulation applies to **all providers, deployers, manufacturers, importers and distributors** who place AI models, AI systems or AI-based services on the Union market or integrate them into their products, **regardless of where they are established and regardless of where their servers sit**. What counts is not where the company is based, but where its output meets the market. The declared aim is the **Brussels effect**, the global reach of EU law. That creates tension in particular with the United States, whose regulatory philosophy, at least at the federal level, is markedly more restrained.

### Substantive limits

As wide as the territorial reach is, so wide are the substantive exemptions ([Art. 2 AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}). Excluded are AI for **military, defence or national-security purposes**, AI used by third-country authorities, AI used exclusively for **scientific research and development**, and pure research, testing and development activities prior to market placement. Also outside scope is the use of AI in the course of a **purely personal, non-professional activity**: the Regulation does not address the private end user. Free and open-source AI is privileged, though not where prohibited, high-risk or generative systems are concerned.

::: {.drag-exercise}
The *marketplace principle* attaches to where the output meets the market, not to where the provider is established; a purely *personal, non-professional* use of AI falls outside the scope.
:::

### What is an "AI system"?

The key definition sits in [Art. 3(1) AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}. An **AI system** is a *machine-based system* designed to operate with *varying levels of autonomy*, that may exhibit *adaptiveness* after deployment, and that, for *explicit or implicit objectives*, infers from the input it receives how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments. Three features carry the definition: **autonomy**, **adaptiveness** and the **inference of outputs** from inputs. Classic, deterministically programmed software therefore falls outside the concept. The wording deliberately tracks the **OECD definition of AI systems** to secure international interoperability. To aid interpretation, the Commission's AI Office published [guidelines](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-ai-system-definition-facilitate-first-ai-acts-rules-application){target="_blank"} on 6 February 2025.

::: {.flip-card}
#### AI system (Art. 3(1) AI Act)
A machine-based system that operates with varying autonomy, may adapt after deployment, and infers from inputs how to generate outputs (predictions, content, recommendations, decisions) that influence physical or virtual environments.
:::

## The risk-based approach

The core idea of the AI Act is simple: instead of treating every AI alike, the Regulation grades its requirements by the assumed **risk** to safety, life and fundamental rights. The result is a pyramid of four tiers. The higher the risk, the denser the obligations; the vast mass of everyday AI stays unregulated.

![The four-tier risk pyramid of the AI Act: unacceptable risk is prohibited outright; high-risk systems face risk-management obligations before they may be placed on the market; limited-risk systems, such as generative AI and chatbots, face transparency obligations; minimal-risk AI remains free from regulation (own illustration).](media/ai-act-risk-pyramid.png){fig-alt="Pyramid with four tiers from top to bottom: Unacceptable Risk; High Risk, with risk management obligations before AI systems are allowed to be put on the market; Limited Risk, with transparency obligations for generative AI systems and chatbots; Minimal Risk, free from regulation." width="80%"}

## Prohibited practices (Art. 5 AI Act)

At the apex of the pyramid sit the practices sometimes called, a little dramatically, the "deadly sins". [Art. 5(1) AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"} bans AI practices deemed a threat to safety, life and fundamental rights. They include in particular:

- **manipulative AI** that uses subliminal techniques to cause significant harm (lit. a);
- AI that exploits **vulnerabilities** (for instance due to age, disability or economic situation) to distort behaviour (lit. b);
- comprehensive, cross-context **social scoring** (lit. c);
- **predictive policing** that forecasts crime solely on the basis of personal profiling (lit. d);
- **emotion recognition** in the workplace and in education (lit. f);
- certain forms of **biometric categorisation** and the **untargeted scraping** of facial images to build databases.

To interpret these bans, the AI Office likewise issued [guidelines](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-prohibited-artificial-intelligence-ai-practices-defined-ai-act){target="_blank"} on 4 February 2025.

The Digital Omnibus added two more prohibitions, and they are the one place where the 2026 amendment *tightens* rather than relieves. New **[Art. 5(1)(ba)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}** bans AI systems that generate or manipulate realistic depictions of an identifiable person's intimate body parts or of that person engaged in sexual conduct without their free, specific, informed and explicit consent, the so-called **"nudifiers"**; new **lit. (bb)** bans the generation or manipulation of child sexual abuse material within the meaning of Art. 2(c) and (e) of Directive 2011/93/EU. Both apply from **2 December 2026**, not from the 2 February 2025 start date of the rest of Chapter II.

Attached to them is a scope rule worth reading closely, because it allocates responsibility along the value chain rather than banning a capability outright. Under **Art. 5(1a)**, placing such a system on the market is prohibited only if the generation is either the system's *intended purpose* or a **reasonably foreseeable and reproducible** output of its design *and* the system lacks reasonable safeguards against that misuse. A general-purpose image generator is therefore not caught merely because someone can coax prohibited output from it; it is caught if that output is foreseeable and the provider built no guardrails. For *deployers* the ban bites only where they actually use the system for that purpose.

### Special case: real-time remote biometric identification

The thorniest point was **live facial recognition for law enforcement**. Here the positions clashed head-on: Parliament wanted a blanket ban, the Council was against it. The result is a **compromise** ([Art. 5(1)(h), (2)-(5) AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}). Real-time remote identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes is **prohibited in principle**, but permitted subject to authorisation in narrow exceptions: to search for a missing person, to avert a concrete and imminent terrorist threat, and to locate perpetrators or suspects of serious crime. Outside these exceptions, remote biometric systems are classified as high-risk and regulated strictly.

::: {.quick-check}
A school application is meant to read pupils' emotions during class in order to measure "attention". How is this classified under the AI Act?

- High-risk AI with conformity assessment
- **Prohibited practice (emotion recognition in education)**
- Limited risk with a transparency duty
- Minimal risk with no specific requirements
:::

## High-risk AI (Art. 6 et seq. AI Act)

Below the threshold of prohibition sits the true centre of gravity of the Regulation. The rules on high-risk AI have their roots in **product-safety law** and transfer its logic to AI.

### Two gateways into the high-risk class

[Art. 6 AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"} knows two points of attachment. Under **paragraph 1**, a system is high-risk if it is used as a **safety component** of a product that is already subject to EU safety law and requires **third-party conformity assessment** (Annex I, for instance toys, lifts, medical devices and motor vehicles). Under **paragraph 2**, it is high-risk if its intended purpose is listed in **Annex III** and, on a case-by-case assessment, it poses risks to health, safety or fundamental rights. Annex III names, among others, critical infrastructure, education (such as exam scoring), employment (such as **CV screening** in recruitment), essential services (such as **credit scoring**), law enforcement, migration, and the administration of justice and democratic processes.

The Digital Omnibus narrowed that first gateway. A component counts as a **safety component** only where its *intended purpose* is to prevent or mitigate risks to health and safety (Art. 3(14) as amended), so the test turns on what the provider designed it *for*, not on where it sits in the product. Art. 6(1a) draws the consequence: AI used solely for user assistance, performance optimisation, automation, usability or quality control is **not** a safety component. Art. 6(1b) closes the obvious gap — systems whose failure *would* endanger health and safety remain safety components whatever their stated purpose. The practical effect: a predictive-maintenance model in a factory is ordinarily outside gateway 1, while the model that decides whether the press stops is inside it.

### The corrective in Art. 6(3)

So that not every trivial application in an Annex III field becomes high-risk AI, **[Art. 6(3) AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}** provides a derogation, and it works in two steps. The system must pose **no significant risk** to health, safety or fundamental rights, in particular because it **does not materially influence the outcome of decision-making** — *and* it must fall into one of four listed categories: a narrow procedural task, improving the result of a completed human activity, detecting decision patterns without replacing the human assessment, or a merely preparatory task. One override cuts across all of it: a system that performs **profiling of natural persons** is *always* high-risk, whatever the rest of the test would say. Providers must **document** their assessment and register the system ([Art. 6(4)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}).

### Providers and deployers

Who is regulated, and how, depends on the role in the value chain. The **provider** is the person who develops an AI system or model, or has it developed, and places it on the market (in everyday terms, the manufacturer). The **deployer**, by contrast, uses the system under its own authority (beyond purely private use). The provider originally determines the intended purpose and can exclude unwanted uses. Decisive is the **reassignment rule** of [Art. 25 AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}: anyone who markets a system under their own name, substantially modifies it, or through actual use puts it to a high-risk purpose **steps legally into the provider's position** and takes on its obligations. The Omnibus sharpened what happens to the first provider: under Art. 25(2) as amended it **ceases to be the provider** of that system but owes the new one cooperation, information and reasonable technical access — and breaching that duty is now itself fineable (Art. 99(4)(da)). **Clarifying one's own role is therefore the very first compliance step.** Test in the simulator below which circumstances turn a deployer into a provider.

::: {.widget}
<iframe src="widgets/kapitel-12/widget-provider-deployer-roleswitch.html" width="100%" height="900px" frameborder="0" style="border:none;" title="Role-switch simulator: deployer becomes provider"></iframe>
:::

::: {.flip-card}
#### Provider vs. deployer
The provider develops an AI system or model and places it on the market; the deployer uses it under its own authority. Under Art. 25 a deployer can become a provider by rebranding, substantial modification, or a change of intended purpose.
:::

### The obligations of providers (Art. 8-15 AI Act)

For high-risk systems a dense catalogue of obligations applies across the whole lifecycle: a **risk-management system** with risk analysis and mitigation before and after market entry ([Art. 9](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}); **data governance**, meaning training only on qualified, representative datasets ([Art. 10](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}); **technical documentation** ([Art. 11](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}); **record-keeping** for traceability ([Art. 12](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}); **transparency** and clear instructions for downstream actors ([Art. 13](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}); **human oversight**, for instance through a stop function ([Art. 14](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"} — the legal codification of the HITL, HOTL and HIC gradations from the unit on ethics guidelines); and **robustness, accuracy and cybersecurity** ([Art. 15](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}), where conformity under the Cyber Resilience Act now counts as compliance (Art. 42(3)).

One of these duties moved house in 2026, and the move matters beyond the high-risk tier. Testing a model for discrimination usually requires the very data that reveals it — ethnicity, religion, health — which Art. 9 GDPR forbids processing in principle. The AI Act's answer used to sit in Art. 10(5) as a narrow permission for providers of high-risk systems. The Omnibus **deleted Art. 10(5)** and re-enacted it as **[Art. 4a](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}** in Chapter I, subject to six cumulative conditions — no workable alternative data, pseudonymisation, strict access control, no transfer onward, deletion once the bias is corrected, and a reasoned record. Two things follow from the relocation. Art. 4a(2) extends the permission to **deployers and to systems below the high-risk threshold**, so far more organisations can rely on it. And because Chapter I escaped the postponement of Chapter III, Art. 4a **already applies** — the permission to test for bias arrived before the obligations it serves.

### Conformity assessment and post-market obligations

Before a high-risk system may reach the market, it goes through **conformity assessment** ([Art. 43-49 AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}): checking against the requirements, registering stand-alone Annex III systems in an EU database, signing a declaration of conformity and, finally, the **CE marking**. Substantial changes trigger the procedure afresh.

![The path of a high-risk AI system to market: from development through conformity assessment, registration in the EU database and the declaration of conformity to placement on the market with the CE marking. Substantial changes lead back to step 2 (source: [EU Commission (2025)](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai), CC BY 4.0).](media/ai-act-conformity-assessment.jpg){fig-alt="Four-step diagram: 1 system developed, 2 conformity assessment, 3 registration in EU database, 4 declaration of conformity and CE marking; substantial changes send the process back to step 2." width="90%"}

After market entry, national market-surveillance authorities take over supervision. **Deployers** must ensure use in line with the instructions, keep logs ([Art. 26 AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}) and, as public bodies and certain private deployers of Annex III systems, carry out a **fundamental-rights impact assessment** before putting the system into use ([Art. 27 AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}). Where a data-protection impact assessment (DPIA) under Art. 35 GDPR has already answered part of that question, the original Art. 27(4) merely said the two assessments should *complement* each other; as amended it now lets the deployer **incorporate or cross-refer to** the relevant parts of the DPIA instead of writing the analysis twice, and Art. 27(5) tasks the AI Office with a questionnaire template. **Providers** set up post-market monitoring; both report serious incidents to the authorities.

::: {.case-study}
#### CV screening in recruitment: high-risk or not?
A medium-sized company introduces an AI that automatically scores incoming applications and produces a ranking of candidates. HR invites only the top ten to interview. How is the system classified, and what follows?

::: {.solution}
Applicant management in hiring is an intended purpose listed in **Annex III** (employment). The system is therefore **high-risk AI in principle** under [Art. 6(2) AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}. The derogation in **[Art. 6(3)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}** cannot rescue it, and the shortest route is the override: scoring applicants is **profiling** of natural persons within the meaning of Art. 3(52) AI Act (which borrows Art. 4(4) GDPR from the unit on profiling and ADM), so the system is *always* high-risk. Even without that, the AI *materially influences* the outcome — anyone outside the top ten is effectively filtered out, which is more than mere support. Consequently, the obligations of [Art. 8-15](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"} apply (among them data governance against discrimination under [Art. 10](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"} and human oversight under [Art. 14](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}), as do conformity assessment with CE marking and the deployer obligations under [Art. 26](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}. The company is initially a deployer here; were it to substantially modify the system or market it under its own name, it would become a provider under [Art. 25](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"} and would bear the full provider obligations.
:::
:::

## Limited risk: transparency duties (Art. 50 AI Act)

One tier lower on the pyramid, the AI Act regulates not the *whether* but only the *disclosure*. [Art. 50 AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"} requires **transparency** wherever people might otherwise be deceived about the nature of an interaction or a piece of content. The content itself is not governed; what is regulated is solely its recognisability. Providers of large generative systems had already reacted to synthetic content with ad hoc technical restrictions, especially before elections, and platforms such as YouTube and Meta had introduced their own labelling requirements; the European legislator's structural answer is instead a binding, harmonised duty that stops short of an outright ban, which would collide with communication freedoms.

| Paragraph | Who | Duty |
|---|---|---|
| Art. 50(1) | Provider | Disclose that a system **interacts** with a person (for example a chatbot). |
| Art. 50(2) | Provider | Mark **synthetic content** in a machine-readable way (watermarking); the technique must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable so far as technically feasible. |
| Art. 50(3) | Deployer | Inform affected persons of **emotion recognition** or **biometric categorisation**. |
| Art. 50(4) | Deployer | Label **deep fakes** and AI-generated text on matters of public interest as artificial. |
| Art. 50(5) | Both | Inform clearly and distinguishably, at the latest at the first interaction or exposure, and accessibly. |

Across all of this, the information must reach the person concerned clearly, distinguishably and at the latest at the first interaction or exposure (Art. 50(5)); the separate demand that the marking technique itself be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable so far as technically feasible belongs to the provider duty in Art. 50(2). Narrow exceptions cover, among others, law-enforcement uses and manifestly artistic, satirical or fictional works. The decisive move in Art. 50 is that the duty attaches to a *role* in the value chain, provider or deployer, rather than to the content alone. Work through the scenarios below to see who owes which disclosure, under which paragraph, and where a narrow exception lets the obligation fall away.

::: {.widget}
<iframe src="widgets/kapitel-12/widget-art50-transparency-mapper.html" width="100%" height="620px" frameborder="0" style="border:none;" title="Art. 50 transparency-obligation mapper"></iframe>
:::

::: {.quick-check}
Under Art. 50 AI Act, an AI-generated deep fake video published by a company must be:

- removed from the platform within 24 hours
- **labelled by the deployer as artificially generated**
- submitted to a conformity assessment before publication
- banned outright as a prohibited practice
:::

### Operationalising Art. 50: the Code of Practice

Art. 50 states obligations but not techniques, and the gap is filled by the **Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content** (Bontcheva, Bechmann et al. 2026), drawn up under the Commission's AI Office as a soft-law interpretive aid. It works on two levels. On the **provider** side it requires two layers of marking: digitally signed provenance metadata following the C2PA standard, and imperceptible **watermarking**, together with a detection tool made available free of charge to regulators, media and researchers, with an interoperability deadline of 2 February 2027. On the **deployer** side it introduces a visible EU icon reading "AI GENERATED" or "AI MODIFIED", to be applied for deep fakes and published AI text at the latest on first exposure, with carve-outs for law enforcement, genuine editorial control in journalism, and art or satire.

The Code is a real step toward closing the **provenance gap**, the absence of a reliable chain of custody for digital media discussed in the unit on discourse and disinformation, but it remains structurally limited. Watermarks can be fragile under compression, re-encoding and cross-model remixing; the "analog hole" (re-recording a screen) defeats embedded signals; and there is as yet no settled interoperability standard across providers. Transparency, in short, mitigates the harm of synthetic reality without dissolving it.

The Digital Omnibus then weakened the Code's legal standing: the original Art. 50(7) let the Commission **approve** such a code by implementing act, and the amended version removes that power. Recital 41 — one of the numbered explanatory paragraphs that precede the enacting terms of every EU act — is candid about why: codes of practice "have limited legal effect and, in particular, do not give rise to a presumption of conformity". What survives is the harder instrument: if the Commission finds the code inadequate it may still lay down **common rules** by implementing act, a binding Commission measure that executes the regulation. For a course that spent two units on the legal quality of soft law, that is an instructive data point.

::: {.details}
#### Deep dive: is Art. 50 a genuine "risk category"?
It is common to draw the AI Act as a four-level pyramid and to slot Art. 50 in as the "limited-risk" tier. That picture can mislead. Art. 50 does not turn on the *size* of a risk at all; it turns on a *capability* of the system, namely its use in communication with people, and high-risk duties continue to apply alongside it (Art. 50(6)). Commentary has also criticised Art. 50(4) for text as poorly drafted: tying the duty to content that "informs the public" on "matters of public interest" produces a paradox in which precisely the contributions most strongly protected by communication freedom are regulated, while gossip is not, and the legislator seems to have had algorithmic journalism in mind rather than the wider field of non-journalistic information. The point for this course is that even a transparency-only instrument raises hard questions of scope and fit — questions the codes of practice under Art. 50(7) are meant to settle in practice, though since the Omnibus they do so without any presumption of conformity behind them.
:::

## General-purpose AI and AI literacy

### GPAI models (Art. 53-55 AI Act)

Large language and foundation models fit poorly into the application-based risk grid, because their purposes are open. The AI Act therefore addresses them separately as **general-purpose AI (GPAI) models**. Under [Art. 3(63) AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}, a GPAI model is one that (often trained on large amounts of data with broad self-supervision) displays significant **generality**, competently performs a **wide range** of distinct tasks, and can be integrated into many downstream systems. Providers of such models must supply technical documentation focused on training procedures and data and inform downstream actors ([Art. 53](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}); two further duties in Art. 53(1) reach directly into the next unit, namely a **copyright policy** that honours rights reservations under Art. 4(3) of the DSM Directive, the text-and-data-mining opt-out (lit. c), and a **public summary of the training content** (lit. d); providers established in third countries must additionally appoint an authorised representative in the EU ([Art. 54](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}).

Tightened obligations apply to GPAI models with **systemic risk** ([Art. 55 AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}): their own risk analysis and mitigation, model evaluation, serious-incident reporting and cybersecurity safeguards. Systemic risk is presumed principally from the **compute used for training**, currently more than 10²⁵ FLOP ([Art. 51 AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}), supplemented by further criteria.

::: {.flip-card}
#### GPAI vs. high-risk AI
High-risk obligations attach to a concrete, risky *intended purpose*; GPAI obligations attach to the *model* itself, whose purposes are open.
:::

### AI literacy (Art. 4 AI Act)

Cutting across all risk tiers is one duty that touches every use. Under **[Art. 4 AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}**, providers *and* deployers must act on the **AI literacy** of their staff and of the persons who operate AI systems on their behalf: the skills, knowledge and understanding for competent use, and an awareness of opportunities, risks and possible harms. Prior technical knowledge, experience, education and the deployment context are to be taken into account. The duty has applied since **2 February 2025** and concerns practically every organisation that uses AI.

The Digital Omnibus rewrote the article, and the change is more than cosmetic. Providers and deployers no longer have to **ensure** AI literacy but to take measures to **support its development**, and Art. 4(1) now says expressly that they need not guarantee any particular level of competence for anyone: an obligation of result became an obligation of effort. In exchange the Commission is to publish practical compliance examples (Art. 4(2)) and the AI Board to adopt recommendations with common objectives (Art. 4(3)). Whether an unenforceable duty plus guidance produces more literacy than an enforceable one is the self-regulation question of the previous unit, now posed inside a binding regulation.

::: {.quick-check}
Under Art. 4 AI Act as amended by the Digital Omnibus, a deployer must:

- guarantee that every employee reaches a defined level of AI literacy
- **take measures to support the development of its staff's AI literacy, without guaranteeing any particular level**
- certify its staff's AI literacy to the market-surveillance authority
- nothing — the Omnibus deleted the AI-literacy duty
:::

## Governance and timeline

### Who watches over the AI Act?

Enforcement rests on a **multi-level governance structure** (Novelli et al. 2024). At the supranational level sits the **AI Office** within the Commission's Directorate-General for Communications Networks, Content and Technology (DG CNECT), which supervises GPAI providers in particular ([Art. 64](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}); it is flanked by the **AI Board** of Member State representatives (Arts. 65-66), an **advisory forum** of stakeholders (Art. 67) and a **scientific panel** of independent experts (Art. 68). At the national level, Member States designate **notifying** and **market-surveillance authorities** (Art. 70); conformity is checked by independent **notified bodies**, the private testing houses accredited to certify that a high-risk system meets the requirements.

### The 2026 shift: enforcement moves to Brussels

The structure just described is the one the AI Act was adopted with, and for AI *systems* it was predominantly national. Not entirely: even the original Art. 75(1) let the AI Office supervise a system built on its own provider's general-purpose model. What the Digital Omnibus changed is the reach and the force of that competence. Under the rewritten **[Art. 75(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}** the AI Office is now **exclusively** competent for two groups: AI systems built on a general-purpose model where model and system come from the same provider *or the same group of companies*, and AI systems that **constitute or are integrated into a very large online platform or search engine (VLOP/VLOSE)** — the largest services, which the Commission designates by decision under the **Digital Services Act**, Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, and supervises directly. Exceptions leave Annex I products, critical infrastructure, law enforcement, border, financial and justice uses with national authorities. In practice the integrated AI of the largest providers now answers to Brussels alone.

The powers are new too. **[Art. 75a](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}** gives the AI Office the toolkit of a market-surveillance authority under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020: investigations, information requests by binding decision, and remote and on-site inspections with rights to enter, copy, question and seal premises. **Art. 75b** lets it declare binding the commitments a provider or deployer offers. **Art. 75c** lets it find an infringement by decision, impose fines under the Art. 99 bands, applied with the necessary adaptations, and levy **periodic penalty payments** — a daily coercive charge that runs until the operator complies, rather than a sanction for the past — of up to 5% of average daily income or turnover per day; the Court of Justice has unlimited jurisdiction over those decisions, and the money flows to the **Union budget** rather than a national one. **Art. 75d** secures the rights of defence.

The design is borrowed from the Commission's direct supervision of very large platforms under the DSA, and it answers a weakness Novelli et al. (2024) had already identified: a regime policed by twenty-seven differently resourced authorities invites providers to gravitate towards the most permissive one. The trade-off is familiar — consistency and capacity against globally operating firms, bought at the price of distance from the national contexts where harms surface.

::: {.flip-card}
#### Who enforces against an AI system?
Normally the national market-surveillance authority. Since the Digital Omnibus, the AI Office is exclusively competent for systems built on the provider's own general-purpose model and for AI inside a DSA-designated VLOP or VLOSE, with powers of investigation, inspection, fines and periodic penalty payments (Art. 75-75d).
:::

### The staggered applicability (Art. 113 AI Act)

The AI Act does not apply in one stroke but in stages ([Art. 113](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}). Four stages were originally envisaged; the Digital Omnibus pushed the two high-risk stages back and added dates of its own. The timeline now in force:

- **2 February 2025**: the **prohibitions** (Chapters I and II) and the AI-literacy duty become applicable;
- **2 August 2025**: the rules on **GPAI models**, the authorities, **governance** and **penalties**, which the Omnibus leaves untouched;
- **27 July 2026**: the Omnibus itself enters into force, and with it Arts. 102-110 AI Act, the amendments to other Union acts (Art. 113, third para., point (d), new);
- **2 August 2026**: the general date of application, and with it the **transparency duties** of [Art. 50](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"} (chatbot disclosure, deep fake labelling);
- **2 December 2026**: a double deadline — the new **Art. 5 prohibitions** on "nudifiers" and AI-generated abuse material apply, and generative systems already on the market before 2 August 2026 must meet the Art. 50(2) marking duty (Art. 111(4), new);
- **2 August 2027**: the Member States' deadline to set up **regulatory sandboxes** (Art. 57), originally 2026; also the deadline for the Commission's delegated acts under the new Art. 2(13), that is, measures by which the Commission may itself amend or supplement parts of the regulation;
- **2 December 2027**: the stand-alone **Annex III high-risk systems** ([Art. 6(2)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}), originally 2 August 2026;
- **2 August 2028**: the **product-related** high-risk systems ([Art. 6(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}), originally 2 August 2027;
- **2 August 2030**: legacy high-risk systems used by **public authorities** must be brought into compliance (Art. 111(2)).

Note what did not move. The general date of application stayed at 2 August 2026, and the postponement reaches only Chapter III Sections 1 to 3: transparency, GPAI, governance and penalties apply on their original dates. So does Art. 6(5), the Commission's duty to issue classification guidelines, deliberately carved out of the delay so that the interpretive aid arrives before the obligations it interprets.

::: {.details}
#### Deep dive: why 2028 for Art. 6(1)?
The product-related high-risk systems (gateway 1) still get the longest grace period, because they must be embedded into the existing conformity procedures of sectoral product-safety law (Annex I, for instance vehicles and medical devices). This interlocking with established testing regimes and notified bodies evidently needed more lead time than first estimated. The Digital Omnibus pushed the Annex III date back by sixteen months and the Annex I date by a further twelve, preserving the original gap between them: the stand-alone use cases (gateway 2) now start on 2 December 2027, eight months before the product-integrated systems.
:::

## Individual rights and penalties

### Two individual rights

At Parliament's insistence, the AI Act goes beyond what is usual in product-safety law and grants two **individual rights**. The **right to lodge a complaint** with a market-surveillance authority arises on suspicion of an infringement and does not require the complainant to be personally affected ([Art. 85](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}). The **right to an explanation** runs against the **deployer**, not the provider, and arises where a decision is taken on the basis of the output of an Annex III high-risk system and **produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects** the person — the same threshold as Art. 22 GDPR in the unit on profiling and ADM. Systems under Annex III point 2 (critical infrastructure) are excepted ([Art. 86](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}).

### Penalties (Art. 99 AI Act)

Member States must provide for effective penalties. The frame is graded: infringements of the **prohibited practices** can be fined up to **EUR 35 million or 7%** of worldwide annual turnover; infringements of other obligations up to EUR 15 million or 3%; and incorrect information supplied to notified bodies or national authorities up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% (in each case whichever is higher). Providers of **GPAI models** fall outside this scheme: their fines are imposed not by Member States but by the **Commission** under [Art. 101](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401689){target="_blank"}, up to 3% of worldwide annual turnover or EUR 15 million.

The Omnibus left these ceilings alone but softened their edges for smaller firms, and it did so unevenly. **SMEs**, including start-ups, were always entitled to the *lower* of the percentage and the absolute figure across all three bands (Art. 99(6)). The new **Art. 99(6a)** extends that relief to **small mid-caps** — the category between an SME and a large company, introduced into the AI Act by the Omnibus in Art. 3(14b) — — but only for the second and third bands, not for the prohibited practices. A small mid-cap that deploys a banned system faces the full 35 million. Art. 99(1) additionally obliges Member States to weigh the economic viability of SMEs and small mid-caps when setting a penalty, and to consider warnings and non-monetary measures alongside fines.

::: {.quick-check}
Which statement about the enforcement of the AI Act is correct?

- The AI Act contains its own claim for damages against AI providers.
- **Infringements of the prohibited practices can be fined up to EUR 35 million or 7% of annual turnover.**
- Real-time remote biometric identification is banned without exception.
- GPAI models are subject to the same obligations as high-risk systems.
:::

## From ethics to law, and on to liability

With this, a large arc of the course closes. In the units on ethics we grounded values such as fairness, transparency and human oversight, probed the limits of machine responsibility, and, with Collingridge and Dignum, demanded that ethical requirements be built into the development process **from the start**. The AI Act is the legal answer to precisely that demand: it translates abstract principles into enforceable obligations across the entire lifecycle of a system. The Digital Omnibus is a reminder that the translation is not finished, and that a regulation can be rewritten while it is still coming into force.

What the Act deliberately leaves out is the question of who pays when an AI causes harm, and who owns what an AI produces. One thread does run from here into that terrain: since 27 July 2026 the AI Act sits in Annex I of the Representative Actions Directive, so consumer bodies can bring collective actions over infringements — a route to enforcement, though still not a claim for damages. Those two questions, intellectual property and civil liability, are the subject of the final unit.
